content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run** example that shows three common ways to create a training / test split for a DataFrame that looks like this:

| column name | type |
|-------------|------|
| `machine_id` | categorical (40 machines) |
| `timestamp`  | datetime (irregularly spaced) |
| 12 numeric sensor columns | float / int |
| `failure_next_24h` | binary target (0 / 1) |

The code uses **only `pandas` and `scikit‑learn`**.  Pick the strategy that matches how you want the data to be split:

| strategy | when to use it |
|----------|----------------|
| **chronological split** | you want a “real‑time” test set (everything after the cutoff). |
| **random stratified split** | you want a representative random sample, preserving the class balance. |
| **group‑by‑machine split** | you want the classifier to have never seen the machines that will be evaluated (avoids any leakage from a particular machine). |

---

## 1️⃣ Load & clean the data

```python
import pandas as pd

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Read the CSV (or any other pandas source)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
df = pd.read_csv(
    "sensor_readings.csv",          # <-- change to your actual filename/path
    parse_dates=["timestamp"],     # parse the timestamp column as datetime
    dtype={"machine_id": "category"}   # keep machine_id as a categorical label
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Make sure the rows are ordered by time (helps with the time‑based split)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
df = df.sort_values("timestamp").reset_index(drop=True)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Define feature / target columns
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
target_col = "failure_next_24h"

# all numeric columns except the identifier / timestamp / target
feature_cols = [
    c
    for c in df.columns
    if c not in ("machine_id", "timestamp", target_col)
]

print(f"\nShape: {df.shape}")
print(f"Target distribution:\n{df[target_col].value_counts()}")
```

---

## 2️⃣ Choose a splitting strategy  

Below are three **self‑contained** blocks.  Comment out the ones you don’t need and keep the one that fits your experimental design.

### ──► A) Chronological (time‑based) split  

```python
from datetime import timedelta

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# Use the earliest 80 % of timestamps for training, the latest 20 % for test
# --------------------------------------------------------------
cutoff = df["timestamp"].quantile(0.80)          # 80‑th percentile of time
print(f"\nChronological cutoff: {cutoff}")

train_df = df[df["timestamp"] <= cutoff]
test_df  = df[df["timestamp"] >  cutoff]

X_train, y_train = train_df[feature_cols], train_df[target_col]
X_test,  y_test  = test_df[feature_cols],  test_df[target_col]

print(f"Train rows: {len(train_df)}   Test rows: {len(test_df)}")
```

> **Why a time‑based split?**  
> Sensor data are usually “future‑looking” – you want the model to never see future information when you evaluate it.  The cutoff above automatically respects the irregular sampling because it simply splits on the timestamp value.

---

### ──► B) Random *stratified* split (preserves the class ratio)  

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# Random 80/20 split, stratified on the binary target
# --------------------------------------------------------------
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    df[feature_cols],
    df[target_col],
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=42,               # reproducible
    stratify=df[target_col]         # keep the 0/1 proportion in each set
)

print(f"\nRandom stratified split:")
print(f"Train rows: {len(X_train)}   Test rows: {len(X_test)}")
print(f"Train target distribution:\n{y_train.value_counts(normalize=True)}")
print(f"Test  target distribution:\n{y_test.value_counts(normalize=True)}")
```

---

### ──► C) Group‑by‑machine split (no machine appears in both splits)  

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# Split *by machine*: e.g. 20 random machines go to test, 80 to train
# --------------------------------------------------------------
gss = GroupShuffleSplit(
    test_size=0.20,          # 20 % of the *groups* (machines) → test
    random_state=42,
    n_splits=1
)

group_train, group_test = next(gss.split(df[feature_cols], df[target_col], groups=df["machine_id"]))

X_train = df.iloc[group_train[feature_cols]]
y_train = df.iloc[group_train, df.columns.get_loc(target_col)]
X_test  = df.iloc[group_test[feature_cols]]
y_test  = df.iloc[group_test,  df.columns.get_loc(target_col)]

print(f"\nMachine‑group split:")
print(f"Train machines: {X_train['machine_id'].nunique()}   Test machines: {X_test['machine_id'].nunique()}")
print(f"Train rows: {len(X_train)}   Test rows: {len(X_test)}")
```

> **When to use this?**  
> If you plan to roll the classifier out to *new* machines at inference time, you want a clean hold‑out of machines you have never trained on.

---

## 3️⃣ (Optional) Put the split data into a scikit‑learn pipeline

If you need the data in the exact format `model.fit(X, y)` expects, you can wrap the preprocessing + model in a `Pipeline`.  This is handy because you’ll reuse the same object later for CV or for the final test prediction.

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression   # <-- any estimator you like

# Example using the **chronological** split from section 2A
model = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1_000, random_state=42))
])

model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# ------------------------------------------------------
# After fitting, predict on the held‑out test set
# ------------------------------------------------------
test_pred = model.predict(X_test)
print(f"\nTest set size: {len(test_pred)}")
print("Predicted class distribution:\n", pd.Series(test_pred).value_counts())
```

---

## 4️⃣ Quick sanity‑check that the three splits are mutually exclusive

You can run **all three** blocks in the same notebook and verify that none of the rows overlap:

```python
# Example after running A, B, and C
def overlap(dfs, name):
    # returns the number of rows that appear in *any* two of the dfs
    from itertools import combinations
    total_overlap = 0
    for a, b in combinations(dfs, 2):
        total_overlap += len(set(dfs[0].index) & set(dfs[1].index))
    print(f"{name}: {total_overlap} duplicated rows across the splits")

overlap([train_df, test_df, df], "all splits")
```

If `0` is printed, you’re good to go.

---

### 🎯 TL;DR – One‑liner for each common scenario

```python
# 1) Chronological 80/20
cutoff = df["timestamp"].quantile(0.80)
train_df = df[df["timestamp"] <= cutoff]
test_df  = df[df["timestamp"] >  cutoff]

# 2) Random stratified 80/20
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(
    df.drop(columns=["machine_id","timestamp"]), df["failure_next_24h"],
    test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=df["failure_next_24h"])

# 3) Machine‑group 80/20
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
gs = GroupShuffleSplit(test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
tr_idx, te_idx = next(gs.split(df.drop(columns=["machine_id","timestamp"]),
                               df["failure_next_24h"], groups=df["machine_id"]))
```

Pick whichever block you need, feed `X_train / y_train` and `X_test / y_test` into your classifier, and you’re ready to model the sensor data! 🚀
